content: 1. In this booklet, we employ a structured approach to guide you through various types of road safety stories. This includes identifying the focus of your story, determining who you should interview, and formulating the right questions to ask. These stories range from straightforward coverage of road crashes to more complex explorations of road safety as a critical public health issue. The list provided is not exhaustive but is intended to help you think about different ways to approach road safety stories in a broader context. 2. A road crash is not merely a random event. Investigate deeply and ask why it occurred. 3. Maintain a record of your road crash stories, reuse the material, establish connections, and look beyond the isolated event. 4. Do not consider a fatal crash as fully covered just because you reported on it when it happened. Follow up on the incident and continue reporting until the causes of the crash have been thoroughly investigated. 5. Do not wait for a crash to occur before writing. Instead, focus on trends and seek expert opinions. 6. To shift from crash reporting to road safety reporting, consider the following: Identify the focus of your story, such as a fatal crash. Speak to police officers, first responders, and police commanders. Ask questions like: What caused the crash? What risk factors were involved? Could the incident have been prevented? What measures are traffic police taking to prevent such situations? What could be done differently? What data systems are in place to record crashes, and are these systems interconnected with other relevant entities? 7. If your story focuses on law enforcement, interview senior police officials, political leaders, legal professionals, and road safety experts. Ask whether road safety laws are consistently enforced. If not, inquire about the reasons, such as lack of resources, corruption, or other barriers. Explore whether traffic police can safely enforce laws and whether measures are in place to protect them from injury while on duty. 8. If your story addresses a specific road safety problem and its potential solution, consult government officials from relevant transport agencies or ministries, as well as road safety experts from academia or NGOs. Ask how the problem is defined, what evidence supports this conclusion, how the issue can be resolved, and whether there is evidence to support the proposed solution. Investigate what neighboring countries have done to address similar issues. 9. For a big picture road safety management story, speak to road safety authorities or boards. Ask who is responsible for road safety in the country, how it is managed, and how the responsible agency coordinates with other governmental institutions. Inquire about areas for improvement, the types of data systems in place, how injuries and fatalities are recorded, who has access to this information, and how the data are used to enhance road safety. 10. If your story focuses on specific groups of road users, such as bicyclists, pedestrians, or taxi drivers, consult road user organizations and individuals who witness the problem, such as street vendors. Ask about the dangers these groups face, how their risks differ from other road users, what data are available, and whether specific legislation or infrastructure could protect them. Investigate best practices in this area and whether they are applicable to your country. 11. If you are exploring road safety as a local public health issue, interview hospital and clinic administrators, health ministry officials, senior police officers, and road safety experts. Ask about the percentage of hospital or clinic intake related to road traffic injuries, the type of care required, the average time patients spend in the facility, the cost of care, and what happens to patients after they leave. Determine what resources are needed to address the problem, such as beds, specialists, operating rooms, X-ray machines, emergency units, or recovery units. 12. For stories on post-crash care services, consult rehabilitation and physiotherapy centers, as well as victims and victims’ associations. Ask what percentage of patients were injured in traffic crashes, the physical challenges they face, how their lives change after a serious injury, and what happens to them after leaving the facility. Inquire about the average cost and duration of services for one injured person. 13. If your story focuses on emergency services, speak to emergency medical service personnel and managers, both private and public, as well as hospital emergency room staff. Ask about the availability and gaps in emergency services, who pays for these services, and the pros and cons of private versus public providers. Investigate the quality of local emergency services and the complications that arise when crash victims are transported by untrained individuals. Determine whether there are laws protecting laypeople who voluntarily assist crash victims from lawsuits. 14. If your story examines standards and technology as part of the solution, consult industry and academic experts, personnel at testing facilities, staff from Global NCAP, consumer groups, police officials, and road safety experts. Ask about the latest technological solutions to prevent certain behaviors or enforce legislation, which vehicle manufacturers have the best safety records, and whether there are laws mandating safety features in vehicles. Investigate the standards for safety equipment, such as helmets, and how local laws compare to international standards. Determine whether these standards are accessible and enforced at both industry and user levels. 15. If your story focuses on the availability and affordability of safety measures or interventions, consult consumer organizations, market research agencies, retailers, and international organizations like Global NCAP. Ask what products are available on the market, whether they meet legal standards, and what consumers think about these products. Investigate consumer attitudes and behavior through market research studies. 16. If you are exploring road safety as a political and development priority, interview politicians from various parties, especially during election periods, as well as officials from relevant government agencies, road safety experts, and NGOs. Ask whether any politicians have made road safety a priority, what issues they are raising, and why they believe it should be prioritized. Investigate the rationale and evidence for making road safety a development priority and whether data support this argument. 17. If your story focuses on alternative transport as a safer and greener option, consult environmentalists, urban planners, and organizations working on sustainable mobility or alternative transport models. Ask about viable transport alternatives in your city, who is promoting them, and the economic and health benefits of these alternatives. Explore the relationship between safer roads and more livable cities, and investigate the concept of sustainable mobility and its connection to road safety. 18. If your story addresses safer roads and better transport infrastructure, consult road safety engineers and infrastructure specialists, including those from the World Bank, iRAP, and the European Commission. Ask how to build roads that are both safe and efficient, the cost of incorporating safety into road construction, and related statistics. Determine who decides on safety norms and how they are implemented. Investigate whether local laws require safety features in new roads and how equitable the traffic and road environment is. 19. If your story focuses on the economic cost-benefit analysis of road safety, consult economists specializing in health costs and development, international organizations, government ministries, investors, and businesspeople. Ask how the cost of prevention compares to the cost of care, the impact of traffic injuries and fatalities on GDP, and how indirect costs are calculated. Investigate the correlation between road traffic injuries and poverty, and whether a poor road safety record deters investors and slows economic development. 20. If your story examines road safety legislation, consult legal experts, legislators, road safety interest groups, police, research organizations, and academics specializing in road safety. Ask what is missing or flawed in the country’s legislation, which countries have the best road safety laws, and what makes a good road safety law. Investigate where to find information on best practices, whether compromises are necessary for implementation and enforcement, and how stakeholder input shapes legislation. Determine whether road safety laws are reviewed and updated, how frequently, and how the public is informed of changes.
